  I got four wrong, but I contest the question about the amount of plastic in the brain.
  
  The degree of scientific confidence that the average healthy person has roughly 5 grams of plastic in their brain is moderate to low.
  
  I'm inclined toward the lower end of that confidence range. The figure is calculated from a relatively small brain sample, which creates problems when extrapolating to the brain's full mass.   The first thing you learn as a teacher is that students have many different preferences on how they learn. Some need visual s, some are purely auditory, some need text/flash cards, and some need 1 on 1 interaction with a human. You can say one style is boring compared to another, but at the end of the day that is your own personal and extremely biased opinion.  Someone who is a visual learner will find flash cards very boring or vice versa. But the important take away is that none of these choices are incorrect. Whats important is that you actually learn it, and if the syle you choose isn't getting sufficient results, just upgrade your methods or try different routes.

    ↳ **@avenotrius4340** (👍0 · 2026-02-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=CFtUtPCdqLA&lc=UgygQRgMPHnDgcPEdFl4AaABAg.ASoCSoFBYH3AT1-J7S6Rut
      learn one language at a time for a few years until you get to b2-ish for each one. its important you do that otherwise you'll mix up languages and barely progress due to scattered focus.
      
      if you learn Spanish first, go for Portuguese next because those two languages are closely related and a lot of your skills in Spanish can directly carry over.
      
      also dont use duolingo it sucks. for German specifically search up 'Nico's Weg'.
      Best one for Spanish would be 'Dreaming Spanish'
      
      look into these two methods for language learning instead of duolingo:
      1) comprehensible input (podcasts, apps, youtube videos).
      2) active recall and spaced repetition. (Anki decks which are especially good for Chinese and Japanese)

  1. What helps me the most is traveling to that country and forcing yourself to speak it with people even if you are shy.
  
  2. Whichever sentence or word you think of automatically in your head when you are doing everyday stuff, translate it to the language you are learning. (The fastest way I learned)
  
  3. Find yourself a friend that speaks that language (or a tutor if there is noone) and talk to them in it and ask everything.
  
  This helped me learn and speak basic conversational Portugese in one month, because I even tried to think in it. And I understood almost everything.
  
  BONUS: watch as many series in that language

  The issue is that if you only learn the Egyptian dialect, for instance, and then travel to Saudi Arabia, people will understand your dialect but respond in their own Saudi dialect, making it difficult for you to comprehend much of the conversation. On the other hand, if you communicate in Modern Standard Arabic, they will reply in the same formal language. Modern Standard Arabic serves as a unifying language across all dialects. Therefore, I believe that anyone aspiring to become a translator, for example, would benefit most from learning Modern Standard Arabic.

    ↳ **@Amiyya-LearnSpokenArabic** (👍0 · 2026-04-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GC2yy_gI6m0&lc=UgyryK4jkLpPtmInxM14AaABAg.ANq8GfOkEmIAVIduTUw6KJ
      This is actually the stage where most learners get stuck.
      You understand everything… but when you speak, it feels wrong.
      That’s because you didn’t learn sentences…
      you learned information.
      Real speech is not grammar + vocab.
      It’s patterns, ready-made phrases, and repetition.
      That’s why natives sound natural…
      they’re not building sentences, they’re using them.

  Also there is a way to get a strong base in general spoken Arabic, Simply use AI and ask it to tell vocab in multiple dialects and select the most common one, If theres no common vocab then use MSA/Fusha one but pronounce it in dialectal way like:
  أريد أروح بکرة
  Areed AruH bukrah
  
  Here you are saying "Areed" which is casualized form of "Ureedu"

      But here’s what most learners realize too late:
      Arabic is NOT about vocabulary.

      Because people don’t speak in mixed Arabic…
      they speak in rhythm, shortcuts, and habits.

    ↳ **@Amiyya-LearnSpokenArabic** (👍0 · 2026-04-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GC2yy_gI6m0&lc=UgyvDb0H-US6ZdP7vYB4AaABAg.ASAgtZZZOwRAVIeFO2AK-Q
      You’re overthinking this more than you need to.
      There’s no “perfect level” in MSA before switching.
      In fact… waiting too long is what slows you down.
      MSA helps you understand structure,
      but real speaking comes from dialect.
      So the best move is:
      start Egyptian now, while continuing MSA lightly.
      Don’t separate them…
      let them support each other.

  Learning Arabic. Why are there numbers included in English translations?? What do they mean? “I’ll-joo3” umm “ill-joo-three”???
    ↳ **@Amiyya-LearnSpokenArabic** (👍0 · 2026-04-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=GC2yy_gI6m0&lc=UgxENhl9S8jq4Jr0T6h4AaABAg.AO-BqleWafzAVIf7fbJAxN
      Great question 
      Those numbers are not random…
      they represent Arabic sounds that don’t exist in English.
      For example:
      “3” = the Arabic letter “ع”
      So “il-jo3” is not “three”…
      it’s actually a sound your mouth needs to learn.
      That’s why reading Arabic like this can be confusing…
      because you’re reading symbols, not sounds.**

      As a native speaker, I often know exactly how something is wrong but not why. While learning Spanish I really enjoyed learning and understanding why something is done a certain way.
      
      I do enjoy learning obscure rules about English though.
      
      One of my favorites is something most native English speakers know naturally but don't know there is a rule regarding it.
      
      Click-clock, pitter-patter, hip-hop. These words are reduplicatives and they always follow the rule of having the smallest and easiest vowel sound in the first word and a larger vowel in the latter.
      
      Smallest and easiest referring to the shape your mouth makes to form the words.

      ​ @DaviAlva420 "definitely me who always..." is not grammatically correct, but it can be used informally on the Internet and it sounds pretty natural, so it's fine. If it was "definitely me, who always..." the comma would make it feel more natural to read, since the pause being absent when you first read it could create a moment of confusion.
      
      "...on grammar tests, but..." the word "tests" definitely has to be plural here, because "always" implies multiple times. It also would have a comma if you want to use proper punctuation(not really necessary in an internet comment since the word "but" would make it easy to interpret that a new clause is starting, even without a comma)
      
      "...but my customers say my English is better..." I'm just assuming you meant for this to be present-tense, but it could also be possible that this happened in the past, but doesn't happen anymore. In that case, it's technically correct already to use past tense, but it's a bit mysterious to use past tense with no explanation. It makes me wonder what happened to your customers or why you don't speak English with them anymore lol
      
      "...who are enrolled in college" "who took a college course" "who go to/went to/are going to college" for this one, it's a bit hard to interpret what you meant to say, but I think there are several ways to say what I think you meant. At first I thought you might be using a slang term, like "who be rolling in college" but you'd have to get that exactly right and you might still sound cringe even if you pulled it off😂
      
      Sorry it's such a detailed response, I just love grammar and picking it apart for fun. I believe that you communicate well in English, even if your grammar isn't school-taught. I love hearing different ways non-native speakers will use English, and sometimes I think incorrect grammar can convey complex emotions and concepts just as well or better than proper grammar. I only include as much detail and specificity as possible, because I know it's what I always want to learn and improve upon when I'm trying to speak my second language

Conversely 109s had very little time to engage in a fight over England and their pilots knew this well; any of their dominance real or imagined was largely negated. Re-joining the Battle to deprive Germany of bombers, of any type, was more important than shooting down 109s.       @LeedsichthysProblem-ij3rq No, otherwise the Tiger 2 would just be considered a different model of the Tiger 1. The Panther 2 was specifically a new Panther design with significant differences over the Panther 1, not just some iterations or changes. The Panther D, G and A were all very similar with a few changes, like the ball mount in the front plate, the addition or subtraction of viewing ports/periscopes and the turret chin or lack of chin. The Panther 2 had more armor across the board and an updated suspension. I probably didn't come close to all of the changes, but the Panther 2 was just a significant change for the tank. Though you could argue the Germans weren't consistent with the designations, for example the Panzer IV D is wildly different to a Panzer IV H to the point that you could probably say that at some point there should have been a Panzer IV II. But from how they did the tank designations, the Panther 2 was a redesign of the Panther. Though not to the extent of the Tiger 1 and Tiger 2, those were much different in design compared to Panther 1 and Panther 2. But the Panther A, D and G were all effectively the same or nearly the same with the same engine, protection and capabilities. 
      
      But as I said, you could legitimately argue that the Panzer III and Panzer IV series went through changes significant enough to also warrant entirely new designations like the Panther 1 to Panther 2, but the Germans weren't consistent with designations. But most militaries are that way. But the entire point is that the Panther 2 is an actual design that existed and was built, albeit only a few. The Lion 2, the Lion 1 was just a design concept and a Lion 2 never is known to have existed in even concept, so it was the most likely answer if nothing else.

      The Maginot Line’s role was operational: secure the Franco‑German frontier and make a direct assault too costly.
      
      French strategy, the Dyle Plan, assumed the main German effort would come through Belgium. That’s why the best mobile forces were positioned to advance there.

      And about the Maginot Line "doing its job" that's an awfully convenient definition. The line wasn't an isolated engineering project; it was part of France's entire defensive system. France committed the 3rd, 4th, and 8th Armies to the Maginot Line, sent its best mobile formations—the 7th Army, 1st Army, and the BEF—into Belgium under the Dyle Plan, and left the crucial Sedan sector mainly to the 2nd and 9th Armies because French doctrine assumed the Ardennes couldn't support a major armored offensive.

      @podiumpirate-i0c  Fair point about the bombing. I overreached when I said one concentrated strike would've crippled the whole German thrust. That was too absolute. The Allies didn't have air superiority, and bombers got torn apart by flak and fighters. Sure, hitting the columns in the Ardennes could've caused delays, but anything beyond that is pure speculation. I'll own that.
      
      But here's where I still push back: none of that means the Maginot Line itself was the problem.
      
      Think about what the Line was actually built to do. It was there to make a frontal assault across the Franco-German border so costly that nobody in their right mind would try it and to free up French forces to fight elsewhere. Germany's own battle plan proves it worked. They stacked only 17 divisions in Army Group C, with no armor at all, against the main fortifications. Meanwhile, the big show: 44 divisions and seven panzer divisions, went around through Luxembourg and the Ardennes. They didn't break through the Line. They went out of their way to avoid it.
      
      The real disasters were French decisions, not concrete. The Dyle-Breda maneuver pulled forces into Belgium. The Second and Ninth Armies were undermanned and badly prepared. The reserves sat in the wrong place. And everyone assumed the Germans couldn't possibly bring a major force through the Ardennes and hit the Meuse that fast. That assumption was catastrophic.
      
      So no, I'm not saying the whole defensive system was a triumph. It clearly wasn't, France fell in six weeks. But the Line did what it was supposed to do in its own sector. The system failed around Belgium and the Ardennes, where the operational plan came apart.
      
      You can't say "the forts held, so French strategy was sound." That's nonsense. But you also can't say "France lost, so the forts failed." That's a category error. Those are two completely different levels of analysis.
      
      The simple truth is that the Maginot Line did its job: it deterred a direct attack on the fortified frontier. What lost the battle was the High Command's doctrine, their deployment choices, and their failure to respond fast enough when the Germans broke through at Sedan. The fortifications weren't beaten, Germany mostly went around them because it was the whole idea. Whenever they tried a frontal assault, they suffered catastrophic setbacks.

    ↳ **@alexotero7105** (👍2 · 2025-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_W-wC36oTqw&lc=UgyoE7GItY6LiOv96Nx4AaABAg.AIBRYJ_VvbHAL8Jdx4V-me
      Not just the cities. Almost every town that has one or two hundred people in most cases has taurine events, whether a running or simply a bullring, it’s extended throughout most of the country. The only exceptions are Galicia, Asturias and Cantabria in the north, which I believe have less than 10 bullrings in big-ish cities that are still operational all the way from Pontevedra to Castro Urdiales.
      
      The reason for this distinction is simple: there is a big ass mountain range separating the North from the main plateau that contains most of the country (in Galicia’s case, it’s mostly a system of smaller mountain ranges that are too fricking close to each other). Due to this geographical situation and the subsequent headaches in communication with other parts of the country (which we still suffer to this day to an extent), the North has developed a substantially different culture in each of its regions compared to Castille or Andalucía (for example) and bullfighting is simply not in our DNA; we are people that have a very close connection to local folklore and our Celt ancestry, so many of our celebrations gravitate around that. Besides, with the growing anti-taurine movement in recent years, the slow death that the practice was going through in the North has accelerated and it’s practically disappeared.
      On a social level, at least in my beloved Galicia, we are very disconnected from the rest of the country mostly because of the Massif and because we are literally the farthest region from the capital. As a matter of fact, we have better relations with Lisbon and the Portuguese populace, given our proximity and our shared history. We generally don’t like Madrid and its people cos we have always been looked down upon by the urban average dude in the big capital. In recent years, tourism in the summer has raised considerably and many from Madrid that spent the summer in the south or in Valencia have started to come to our region for their holidays. Needless to say, not all of them are the most respectful bunch - In fact, the visitors we get from abroad are generally kinder to us than them, but it is what it is. Sorry for the rant guys.
      
      I’ve been to Navarre a couple times, but never happened to be there in San Fermín. I hope to see it one day.

  Lift on a plane is a combination of Newton's third law of motion and Bernoulli's Principle. The wing must attain an angle of attack to generate Newtonian lift. Think of as Bernoulli makes a hole in the air and Newton pushes the wing into it. A wing could attain enough lift using Bernoulli only, but only at incredibly large airspeeds. 46/50.
    ↳ **@ChockHolocaust** (👍2 · 2026-02-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PVoRP358HxA&lc=Ugynhjblhxb67e95lYl4AaABAg.ALf355k1lMYASY6vY2aBQv
      Correct. Otherwise a split flap of the type found on aeroplanes such as the Supermarine Spitfire and the Douglas DC-3 would not work. Specifically, a split flap deflects air downwards, which then makes the wing push upwards, rather than creating a difference in airflow speed over the upper and lower wing surface as most other flap types do when either increasing camber, or area, or both. Since a split flap doesn't alter these things, this means it has to be using the third law of motion rather than the bernoulli principle. You can in fact tell this when you drop split flaps because they induce a significantly greater pitch down of the nose than most other types of flap, as a result of an increased  force acting on the rear of the wing. It also explains why split flaps are better for landing than for take off, since they also generate a lot of drag but no actual aerodynamic lift in the way other flap types do, but since you are flying 'downhill' when landing, this doesn't really matter and in fact is somewhat advantageous in preventing an increase in acceleration from essentially being in a dive.

    ↳ **@christopherpardell4418** (👍0 · 2026-03-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PVoRP358HxA&lc=Ugynhjblhxb67e95lYl4AaABAg.ALf355k1lMYATkvvQZ0ChO
      Wings do not generate lift. They generate a downwards thrust. The Bernoulli effect does create a zone of low pressure above the wing, but the plane has too high an inertia for this low pressure to have much effect on it. Rather, well above this low pressure zone is an ocean of air at a higher pressure and each air molecule has very low inertia.  This causes air to rush into this low pressure zone from above, accelerating a mass of air towards the wing, but as that air arrives the wing has moved out of its way and so it rushes downwards just behind the wing. The wing has to continuously accelerate enough air to a thrust matching or exceeding the mass of the plane to fly, and this is why as altitude increases, planes must fly faster to compensate for the lower mass of thinner air.  The angle of attack simply increases the drop in pressure over the wing, causing higher accelerations of the air.  
      Propellors are just wings spinning in a circle, and they obviously produce thrust… not lift.   While the AoA of the underside of the wing creates a high pressure zone, and this air starts to accelerate downwards in the relatively lower pressure air below, this effect is only a minor component of flight because its a small volume of high pressure air and that pressure dissipates rapidly as it expands,  but the ambient pressure air well above the low pressure zone above the wing is the entire atmosphere of higher pressure and it is not significantly diminished by rushing into the lower pressure zone created by the wings motion.  This is why you can hang any number of objects under the wing, but the upper surface needs to be clear.

    ↳ **@davidcarper269** (👍6 · 2025-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PVoRP358HxA&lc=UgyP3SC5Blf5IJzdq4l4AaABAg.AKgsTlzE5FDAKmZaqkdFQR
      Yes, you are correct; a Red Dwarf (more properly "M-type") is on the Main Sequence. It is (relatively) cool, and it is small, but it is NOT "cooling".
       
      As for "Meteor/Meteorite", the process goes "Meteroid" - a small rock in space. "Meteor" - a rock or particle glowing in the Earth's atmosphere. "Meteorite" - A Meteor that has reached the ground. So yes, a Meteorite started out larger than the average Meteor, but it's the fact that it is on the ground that is the definition.

      @wondzellbob9901  number one: Not all planes can fly upside down for more than a few seconds. Number two, when planes DO fly upside down they adopt  a nose high attitude so that the wing is still at a positive angle of attack, even though inverted.   The pilot, upside down, literally has to push the stick forward ( which right side up would put him into a dive )  so that the leading edge of the upside down wing stays HIGHER than the trailing edge  relative to the oncoming air.    This inverses the position of the low pressure area to the underside of the wing, which is upside down. so STILL creating low pressure Above the wing relative to gravity.   Military and stunt aircraft generally have wings that are closer to symmetrical above and below the chord and rely on angle of attack to determine which side of the wing is creating the low air pressure.    But again, the low pressure does NOT ‘suck’ the plane up into the air.   Rather the low pressure zone causes the Ambient pressure air above it to Accelerate into the low pressure zone. As it arrives in the low pressure zone the wing has moved out of its way, thru Generating a downwards Thrust beyond the trailing edge of the wing.   Wings do NOT produce ‘lift’.  Any propellor or cooling fan proves they produce Thrust perpendicular to their proper motion.

  #8 - This is incorrect; blue whales have incredible migration periods in which they will go weeks, even months without eating. Once they reach a feeding ground in summer months they will eat massive amounts of krill everyday.
  
  #20 - Some people have issues with this question, the snake still uses its tongue relative to the other answers. But snakes can also smell through their nose, it's just not the primary means like for hunting.
  
  #21 - Some people claim the Siamese answer is wrong, it is correct. The Balinese is a long-haired version of the Siamese.
  
  #42 - This one is incorrect. Ants are roughly 2.5 million per human on earth though numbers could've been updated since then... but the true answer is flies, or at least categorically  speaking. Flies are a type of flying insect that compose of gnats, mosquitoes, and the common house fly. There's over 17 million flies per human on earth.

  48 points. The WE2 question is a bit complicated, classically Poland is the correct answer as the Geraman invasion of Poland started the European part of WW2 however the Asian part had started 1937 so technically one could argue that Austria would be the first one. Anyway WW2 only became a proper world war in 1941 when Germany declared war on the USA in the aftermath of Pearl Harbor as prior to that there had been two separate wars.   as marcseigar states, there were a couple of events that qualify as invasions in WW II. The 'Anschluss' Austria's is technically an invasion, but no shots were fired, and it did not trigger a declaration of war on Germany. 
  Neither did the invasion of the Sudetenland, or the exchange of gunfire there in March '39. The commonly accepted kick-off date of 1 September was just another exercise in brinkmanship, until GB declared war on Germany two days later.
  However, they failed to declare war on the SU, when the Red Army marched into Poland two weeks later and took the half of the country the Germans hadn't taken.
  
  So technically, a case can be made that Germany's invasion of France in '40 was the first invasion at the time the war was on.

**@sarahsander785** (👍54 · 2025-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nicgq7WLESU&lc=UgyxtIhH7iPvyK7IWQZ4AaABAg
  What people sometimes forget is that punctuation carries meaning. It's not just the words within the sentence, it's the spaces between them, the blocks they form and the little signs that break them up. I use full stops not only to indicate the end of a sentences, but the end of an action.
  "He stood up, breathed in, turned around and looked his brother in the eye." has a slightly diffrent meaning then "He stood up. He breathed in, turned around and looked his brother in the eye." even though the words and actions are the same. But having a full stop focus the readers attention to that specific part of the action, lets them stop for a moment and indicates a short pause in the action of the character. It makes it abundantly clear that he first stood up and paused a bit before he breathed and turned around, while the comma indicates it all happening in short, direct succession or even at the same time.
  This is a thing I fight over with my editor right now, as she wants longer, flowing sentences, where I used a full stop to indicate this little diffrence in time.
  
  Also: Read your story out aloud as a step in the editing process. It helps so much. Reading the sentences aloud forces you to actually read every word and regard every punctuation mark. It lets you find clunky sentences, bad repetitions, too similar characer voices and sometimes even plotholes so easily.

  The problem with this is that the way of writing is the voice, dynamically emerging from years of writing; these writers did not sit and think about constructing sentences in a specific way, they didn't meditate on verbs, they had a liking to a certain form and wrote sentences by it. So it's hard studying these and use them for anything, the voice and style is something which grows from the individual. It's good for absolute newcomers to writing, but the fact is that writing and reading, writing and reading, writing and reading... is all there is to it. After a while, you find the voice, you influence yourself by other's writings. 
  
  The master authors used in teaching writing, rarely went through a writing class, they may have studied other things, history, art, philosophy etc. but writing they evolved themselves, for themselves, and now we use them as examples, rather than evolving our own writing as they did.

  My favorite sentence from Kurt Vonnegut's 'God Bless You Mr. Rosewater' requires some context. The context:
  
  ---
  
  "This is the Rosewater Foundation. How can we help you?"
  
  "Mr. Rosewater—" said a woman, "there was a thing on the radio about you."
  
  "Oh?" Eliot now began to play unconsciously with his pubic hair. It was nothing extravagant. He would simply uncoil a tight spring of it, let it snap back into place.
  
  "It said they were going to try to prove you were crazy."
  
  "Don't worry about it, dear. There's many a slip betwixt the cup and the lip."
  
  "Oh, Mr. Rosewater—if you go away and never come back, we'll die."
  
  "I give you my word of honor I'm coming back. How is that?"
  
  "Maybe they won't let you come back."
  
  "Do you think I'm crazy, dear?"
  
  "I don't know how to put it."
  
  "Any way you like."
  
  "I can't help thinking people are going to think you're crazy for paying so much attention to people like us."
  
  "Have you seen the other people there are to pay attention to?"
  
  "I never been out of Rosewater County."
  
  "It's worth a trip, dear. When I get back, why don't I give you a trip to New York?"
  
  "Oh God! But you're never coming back!"
  
  "I gave you my word of honor."
  
  "I know, I know—but we all feel it in our bones, we smell it in the air. You're not coming back."
  
  ---
  
  And now comes my favorite sentence:

The geography somehow creates a storm almost 160 days a year and it has the most yearly lightning strikes of any place on the planet. The storms used to be so predictable the Spanish sailors called it the Catatumbo Lighthouse because the lightning could be spotted from hundreds of miles away at sea. It’s a popular form of storytelling in the east and is highly addictive: we love symmetry. The Bible is also written as a chiasm, from Genisis to revelation, as well as many stories, like Noah, or Moses, or Daniel, all told as perfect chiasms.   For many years, I've had two addenda to your "power words" and descriptive words. Sentences are more powerful if you can place your most powerful words at the beginning or the end of a sentence, just as a comedian waits until the end of a joke to give you the punch line. As for descriptive words, many writers try to make adjectives and adverbs to all the work. Look for vivid nouns and verbs, or nouns and verbs that evoke images of action.

  2 things.
  1. Could you pin a list of those constructions in the comments; the auction went so fast I forgot to place a bid.
  2. I disagree with banning passive sentences for two reasons. One, if the character being described views the world passively, the passive voice is a way to quietly add that concept to the story. And two, using only active verbs makes digressing from SVO hard. It can be done by changing the mood (interrogative, imperative) and occasionally something like '"The dog," he said.' (OSV) There is far less justification for linking verbs (to be). In other words, with SVO active voice sentences, it becomes a challenge to find what can be added to the front of the sentence to create variety, thereby creating its own monotony.

  A lot of these sentences are awful. Like the Elementary Particles one, it can just as well be describing e.g., someone simply getting older, especially when just being contrasted to fading youth. A lot of these sentences are like that, using excessive and confusing language in order to spend more time communicating less clearly. This was an especially atrocious example, using 20 words to say less than what could be said in 1.
  
  As an aside, some of these sentences are pretty horrifying for other reasons as well. Like this woman who, by the time she was studying mice's mental reward structures, didn't think they could feel fear? What the fuck? Makes me think of stories of those old zoo apes they raised in concrete enclosures, making their brains atrophy. How starved for interaction with non-humans would an adult have to have been for their whole life to be so old and still think something like that?       They were not teaching you "Cats are fast today"  that would be useless for most people in most situations. They were trying to teach you 
       "[Noun] is/are [adjective] [moment]".
      
      If you are able to remember that sentence about cats and learn more words you could say "Internet is slow today" or "Anne is happy" or "Apples are expensive now".
      
      Neither Duolingo nor another app can't teach you every possible sentence. But Duolingo is very good teaching patterns through silly phrases that stick to memory.

**@oroelf** (👍85 · 2025-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=f7SrDSN2Dy8&lc=UgwVroOjBK5HTANQ2Wt4AaABAg
  I have an 1100+ day streak on Duolingo learning Spanish and I'm currently between B1 and B2.  In the early stages Duolingo was actually good at teaching you concepts with their hints at the beginning of a chapter, but as you get further in, the best you get is some examples and it's up to you to figure out things on your own.
  
  I've been using Airlearn since November 2024 (they had a black Friday special) and it has been pretty repetitive for me since my Spanish is already at a certain level, but as I've gotten deeper into the lessons it's actually teaching me concepts that Duolingo never did.  (Such as when to use Que vs Cual)
  
  I'm currently in Section 4 of the Spanish course on Airlearn, and while it hasn't really delved into anything but the present tense, if it maintains the same level of instruction as it has up until now it may surpass Duolingo for me.  Maybe it's because I already understand most of the vocabulary and concepts it's teaching, but I have learned some new vocabulary and I'm curious to see how it approaches the past tense and more advanced concepts.

      I am learning French at the moment. My strategy is a lot of language exposure (reading an online French newspaper every day on the bus on my way to work and back, and watching YouTube videos), and speaking once a week with a native French speaker on italki. I occasionally look at conjugation tables, but I don't go out of my way to study them or learn them by heart. While I agree that nobody in France will ever ask you to conjugate a verb, my ability to communicate successfully in my French conversation classes is somewhat compromised by my lack of mastery when it comes to conjugating verbs. If I had more time to invest, I might do some specific exercises on verbs and their conjugations (in context, of course).

  Duolingo's methodology is based on (Comprehensible input). The lack of explanations for sentences is very simple, when you try to do something and make mistakes several times and then you succeed, and you understand the logic of the sentence, you are more likely to remember this pattern. Imagine that you are playing a game where there are obvious clues, it is unlikely that you will be interested in such a game, and you will learn something.

  I will stay with Duolingo, thanks. The main reason is that I will mostly just remember the overall meaning of the sentence (like. She likes reading.) and everytime I see this sentence I would be blindly guessing just by the overall sound. I tried one app, which was teaching me some sentences like "this is my father", "this is my brother" or sth like it, in Thai. I could not read Thai, so for sure I was not reading those sentences, and also I didn't know what word was exactly what, but because I remembered the first or second "sound" I could just blindly guess the meaning, without really getting it. In Duolingo, the weirder sentence the better, I need to stop and think on each word, I could check each word separately for the meaning and also learn more patterns just by having them switch some words around. As long as the other apps teach you the "regular" sentences that just loop around, I will probably just stick to Duo. But of course, people are different, and maybe this approach works better for them.

**@stiobhardgruamach1368** (👍0 · 2026-08-10) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=f7SrDSN2Dy8&lc=UgzKVPtiQQ7NmulPsL54AaABAg
  The problem with Duolingo is not that its 2012 technology that has never changed significantly. It is that its basically a revival of 1950s behaviorism with a shiny new digital interface... 
  
  The same pedagogy that makes your parents turn a sickly green as they recall their anxieties about high school french and Spanish when they were in school in 1958. The same strategy that makes me want to smash my android phone with a hammer every time it nags me with its incessant ring in the middle of the night while I'm in bed. The same teaching theory that did grotesque experiments on dogs and rhesus monkeys that we all watched in first year psychology. 
  
   And this is problematic not only because you will not learn anything or because it is an absolute motivation killer...  But that it has pushed itself on gullible but well meaning parents who consider it not as a supplement to their teenagers education but as a replacement for it.
  
   If it worked it would be one thing, but it doesn't. If anything it exists to distract you from actually learning. But it's horrifically dehumanizing in the way it frames the conversation on education. 
  
  So we do not need Duolingo, or Duolingo clones like Anki. We need to be talking about how to replace these Christian nationalist funded strategies to erode education and look for tools that actually empower people towards being enthusiastic about life long learning.

  Technically, dude, Elysium IS part of the Hellenistic Underworld. Covered in the indie game Hades, there are three layers to the underworld, and where the soul of the departed went was based on how the gods viewed their lives. If they were looked on favorably, and deemed as heroes, they went to the Elysium Fields to partake in eternal bliss and to relive the glory of their battles. If they were deemed as not worthy of the gods' attention or recognition (the vast majority of the population), they were sent to the Asphodel Meadows, where the departed soul would have to drink from the river Lethe and forget everything about their identities (which is definitely a very frightening Hell if you think about it). If the gods thought you acted reprehensibly, refused to honor them in your life, or wronged them in any way like Tantalus, Prometheus, or Sisyphus, you were sent to Tartarus for your crimes to burn and be punished by the Furies for your crimes.

      Slightly wrong, the Styx IS the boundary of the worlds of the living and the dead, and the dead wait at her banks. While Charon does ferry the dead across the Acheron, this is because it is the principal river of the underworld, which all rivers sprang from.     ↳ **@sofiavelkou1513** (👍1 · 2025-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=8d-tpiFzizk&lc=UgxTU00p0mvIpPtgn0l4AaABAg.AH73lJ-i7iIAIrszqDo-U2
      Virgil names the Styx as the “main river of the Underworld” and claims that all the others flow from it. Ancient texts by Euripides, Aeschylus, and Plato mention Acheron and not the Styx as the river through which Charon transports the dead to the Underworld.

  Can you imagine the staggering losses of each battle in the Civil War? Those are high casualty rates because back then they could only fire one shot every 30 seconds and had to reload the gun powder and bullet all by hand every single shot. The muskets only had a maximum firing range of 75 yards, unless you were equipped with a rifle and the state of the art mini ball at the time, which was a bullet that stayed straight once fired and spiraled out of the rifle once shot. It had a maximum firing range of up to 300 yards and caused way more damage to the body than traditional round bullets.

      In cricket, a wicket can mean all of these 3:
      1. the space between which the 2 batters run (aka the "pitch")
      2. the on-strike batter (when a bowler gets the batter "out", he "takes a wicket". Also, the batting team "loses a wicket")
      3. the 3 stumps+2 bails behind the on-strike batter (if a ball hits the stumps or bails, a commmentor might say "the ball smashed into the wicket")

      @CliveFTP   I was going to gaslight them all by pointing out that when the commentators come out to check out the state of the wicket, they only look at one thing!
      
      But fun fact... actually, Brian is right. Technically, the pitch is just that - the pitch. In the official laws of the game published by the MCC the pitch is defined as that 22 yard rectangular area people bowl on, and makes no use of the term 'wicket'. Whereas, in the law on the 'wickets' they are defined as the set of three stumps at each end. At no point in the laws are the terms 'wicket' and 'pitch' used interchangeably.
      
      Referring to the pitch as "the wicket" is a sporting colloquialism, not technically a correct offical cricket term.

      I am a native greek and the word hierarchy is greek not latin. Derived from  (hierárkhēs, “high priest”) +‎  (-ía, noun-forming suffix). By surface analysis, (hierós, “holy”) +‎ (-arkhía, “rule, government”).  Anyway, vibrant is latin but the explanation energetic is greek (hahahaha)
      
      The word enigma is latin but derived from ancient greek .
      From Latin aenigma (“riddle”), being derived itself from the Ancient Greek verbal noun αἴνιγμα (aínigma, “dark saying, speaking in riddles”).

    ↳ **@stevedallas4942** (👍3 · 2025-12-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vxkG6EEmZKc&lc=UgxWvzcOjMiOfRa7fNp4AaABAg.AIVwKB5QM4AAQAebrUXlWF
      I can relate. 
      In the early 2000s (2003 maybe) there was a circa 1936 Kansas 8th Grade graduation exam circulating around the Internet. 
      Out of curiosity, I contacted the librarian of the school from which my grandfather completed 8th Grade in 1937. She found the final exam in the archives and copied it for me. 
      I took the test and let my Great-aunt ( a teacher for 36 years, but 25 years retired at the time) grade it. 
      I scored a 91% with my deficiency in the math portion. However...
      She pointed out that my wrong answers were of questions in weights and measures not taught to my generation, and regraded on that curve. 
      My score increased to a 98%. She did not regrade some foolish errors where I clearly didn't pay attention.
      
      I gave that exam to three teachers at the highschool where I worked. One is a PhD in child psychology and had been my own Gifted Program teacher in Grades 4 through 6. Another had a Master's in English and 20 years as a teacher. 
      The Third a Bachelor's in History, but my own age.
      
      They all passed. The first two with perfect scores, the last with the same results as myself (but errored on different questions). Neither of us had been taught farming measures like how many bushels to a peck, etc.
      
      Finally I passed it around as a joke in the teacher's lounge...
      Our (furious) Principal, "Doc"  (formerly a PE teacher), scored around an 85. One young Math teacher blew it away with a perfect score (she'd also once been Valedictorian of the same highschool).
      But as for the majority of the faculty that took the challenge, most barely earned a C. Note: they were all under 30, but two were working on their Master's.
      Several were found in the trash and one of those balled up and hurled into the garbage can in front me. That teacher insisted there was no way this ever an exam for 13 year olds and that I was scamming everyone. 
      
      Point? Each Decade since the end of WW2 has been given more opportunities to go to higher grade levels, and learn less....
      Then held to a lower standard while doing so.

      It's my understanding that grammar is mechanics of language, while vocabulary is the parts. One could have flawless grammar with a small vocabulary. Regardless, I believe that the root cause of the decrease in vocabulary is the availability of online entertainment, available 24/7. When I was a boy, a rainy day meant a day curled up reading a book of pirate stories, Poe's gothic tales, or even thumbing through the encyclopedia.  My parents were working class, but to them, books were an escape into other times or a view into places they would never be able to visit, especially my mum.  Judging from my attachment to my PC screen today, I have no doubt that I would have been every bit as illiterate and technically cloistered as the boys of today are.  We must not view them with distain, but with acceptance that the world is a very different place than it was for us.

  Love these! Here's a couple...
  
  Three square meals a day - meaning, a well-fed situation.
  
  Origin: The English navy issued all sailors a "square". Which was simply a stout, square wooden plank. Three times a day? Slop ladled on.
  
  That came out of left field - meaning, an unexpected, kinda crazy idea.
  
  Origin: Chicago Cubs, West Side Ball Park, pre-1915 
  
  West Side park was about a mile West of downtown Chicago. Right next to a burgeoning medical center. Immediately adjacent (behind) the left field stands was the "mental asylum". Often, as baseball games were in progress, loud shrieks and crying came from the woebegone inmates. The phrase, "that came out of left field" was born.
  
  Keep on doing these. They're awesome!

**@twylanaythias** (👍1 · 2025-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MjAznp6cE9E&lc=UgxHkDP5uGWM0YobHuB4AaABAg
  Correction:  "Bite the bullet" has nothing to do with battlefield medicine, and actually goes much MUCH farther back.  In fact, the phrase is actually "bight the boullet" and it originated in later Medieval France.
  
  Though most commonly used from 1000 AD to 1500 AD, the French continued to use slings in combat as late as the early 1700s.  "Bight" (formerly "byht") refers to a loop, bend, or similar portion of a rope or cord which is used to secure something; "boullet" refers to a small piece of stone (or, later, metal) which had been shaped to use as a projectile weapon.  Being given the order to "bight the boullet" was akin to the more modern phrase "lock and load".
  
  In formal Medieval warfare, it was common for leaders to meet before combat to discuss their respective situations - each accompanied by a small retinue of soldiers.  Slings were the dominant projectile weapon of the era (yes, bows were coming into vogue, but they were expensive to acquire in large numbers and required extensive training to use well - slings were cheap and most everyone learned to use one in childhood) and it was easy to tell from a glance if one was 'loaded' in anticipation of use.  For the attending soldiers to have their slings loaded was a non-subtle announcement that they were committed to their mission and unwilling to compromise.

  Sometimes idiom origins are unbelievable because they are not true. I'm 99% sure that is the case with the supposed Hindu origin of "butter someone up." The word butter was used to refer to lavish praise or flattery as far back as the 1600s and held the same meaning as 'butter up.' The word up is often added as an intensifier, so nothing unusual there. The word oil was also used similarly and so was the word sugar. More likely, the Hindu origin is a bit of folk etymology and the true origin is just less interesting and, well, unbelievable. Butter is certainly important in the Hindu religion. It's so important that singling out that one practice as the coinage of an English idiom seems to be a bit too neat and tidy.
  
  It's curious that if you search for information on the Hindu practice of 'throwing' butter at statues of Gods, you will only get references pertaining to it being the origin of the English idiom butter up. That is usually a sign of something amiss. They did anoint statues with butter and used butter in other ways but to "throw balls of butter (or ghee)?" Just blue-skying here, but I'm going to question whether anyone would ever THROW something at a God, even butter or ghee. Don't think this would win favor.

      It's actually both of those things...and a little more. It's more than simply having a hidden agenda, and it's more than simply having an issue with someone else that you need to settle. It's generally used to describe an issue you have with someone else that isn't necessarily obvious to everyone. There's also a fairly heavily implication that the issue you have with the other person / group either isn't entirely justified, that the issue is something others would consider largely unimportant / irrelevant, or that you're taking the issue too personally and your need for vengeance / retribution exceeds what the issue actually requires. 
      
      That being said, of the three options provided, the hidden agenda option was the best fit.

  I'm totally blind and I use a screenreader. In future, if you do another quiz like this, where you've got scrambled letters, could you possibly just read out the letters as well as leaving them on screen? Even without knowing the available letters, I got almost all of the five-letter words, about three-quarters of the six-letter words, and the last three seven-letter words, but my vocabulary is also fairly strong. Hell, I just did this for fun. But yeah. All you'd have to do in order to make this sort of quiz totally accessible to the blind or visually impaired would be to add a little extra reading each time it comes up. Example, making this up from whole cloth. "Number 5. An adjective that means cloudy or unclear. Your letters are u-y-k-m-r." Of course, if you have letters missing, that's fine too, and you can say as much.   A "Bromide" is indeed a chemical compound, however, it is not by default a base--just anything containing bromine. "Labile" however (speaking as a chemist) is not the same as "volatile". A volatile solvent easily evaporates (hexanes, diethyl ether etc.) but when something (let's say a functional group or protecting group) is acid-labile, (or base-labile, etc.) it means the group can be removed from the rest of the molecule (deprotected) by acid (or base) to expose the reactive part of the molecule.

      @zakmartin  Sorry, but no. Bromine (Br2) is the molecular form of the element found in nature and forms a weak acid in water.       His answer was an alkaline chemical and is not correct since bromide compounds can range from strongly acidic to weakly alkaline, although most are neutral.

      Wikipedia:  A bromide ion is the negatively charged form (Br−) of the element bromine, a member of the halogens group on the periodic table. Most bromides are colorless. Bromides have many practical roles, being found in anticonvulsants, flame-retardant materials, and cell stains.[3] ...
      
      Dissociation of bromide salts
      Bromide salts of alkali metal, alkaline earth metals, and many other metals dissolve in water (and even some alcohols and a few ethers) to give bromide ions. The classic case is sodium bromide, which fully dissociates in water:
      
      NaBr → Na+ + Br−
      Hydrogen bromide, which is a diatomic molecule, takes on salt-like properties upon contact with water to give an ionic solution called hydrobromic acid. The process is often described simplistically as involving formation of the hydronium salt of bromide:
      
      HBr + H2O → H3O+ + Br−

      @doreenwhitehead4224  The Romans didn't directly bequeath many words at all to English. The Britons who lived here (I'm in England) when the Romans invaded/settled were Celts and spoke a language similar to Welsh. English came to Britain after the Romans had gone, with the Anglo-Saxons, and it wasn't influenced by Latin. Words like "fainéant" and thousands of others came into English directly from French in the 300 hundred years or so that followed the Norman conquest in 1066, not  from Latin, although, of course, French is a Romance language derived from Latin. Most of the Latin (as opposed to French) words in English came in from Tudor times onwards,

  So many responses from seniors like me. I'm a 79 year old retired elementary school teacher. I've seen a continuous decline in children's vocabulary. Some of it is normal. Times change and certain words become obsolete. But some of it is due to a decline in reading for pleasure. I always ended my school day with a 15 minute read aloud session. My students were 8-10 year olds for whom a chapter book would be a challenge. By sharing a book every afternoon we could review the story, talk about unfamiliar vocabulary and reflect on the actions and motivations of the characters. Two of the most favorite read alouds were Little House in the Big Woods and Ramona the Pest. How do I know? Because those two somehow always mysteriously disappeared from my classroom. I replaced them many, many times over the years. Unfortunately, kids today have replaced books with phones and iPads. They don't have the opportunity to imagine in their minds the stories that they read in books. There are certain things that technology does very well. But in the case of books, reading and vocabulary development, technology has not made improvements.

    ↳ **@ronnielee33** (👍7 · 2025-08-12) — https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=VeC0B1yMOVo&lc=UgyUQLuplkl4EqcTtrF4AaABAg.A9ZIT3klTZoABtiBr7-FTk
      I once saw my friend's 5th grade son in a store. He looked unhappy. I asked him how he was, and he said, "Not good." I asked him what was wrong. He told me that his teacher told him that if he didn't pass his spelling test the next day, she was flunking him. I asked him if he was studying, and he sadly said that it didn't matter, he'd never passed a spelling test in his whole life. He told me he really wasn't very smart. I said that I could teach him a trick that would help, if he liked. One of his words was 'science' ( he showed me). I asked him if he knew Spanish vowels (though English was his first language, we have a lot of Spanish-speaking friends and neighbors); he did know them. I told him that he had to decide, with each word, which  he wanted to use--he chose Spanish. I told him to look at the word and tell me what it said, and he did. Then I asked him to look at it again--does it have a 'k'--no, of course not. Now look at it and pronounce EVERY LETTER. Pronounce the 'C' as if it were a 'K' and pronounce all consonants hard. 'Science' becomes 'Skee-ayn-say.' You know it doesn't have a 'k,' so that's a 'c.'  Spanish vowel system : ah, ay, ee, oh, ooh (a,e,i,o,u). The next day, he tracked me down to tell me he got a B+. The first spelling test he ever passed. The first B+ he ever got.
      
      Sometimes, teachers forget that some kids learn differently. Sometimes, teachers forget to teach differently, or can't seem to learn how. 
      
      That kid? The one that told me that he wasn't very smart? He is a ferry boat captain who is employed by our state. He's had to pass an awful lot of tests to do that. Don't give up.

  I compared the word boredom and ennui with Google ngrams. The word, boredom,  is about ten times as common as the word ennui. That surprised me. My sense of it is that I encounter the word ennui less than once a year. I expected ennui to be much less common than the word boredom than it was.
  
  Ngrams shows the word ennui and the word boredom being about equally common in 1912, After that, boredom became much more common. I am old, but I wasn't around for the heyday of ennui as an English word.
